newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Kurd leader to drop ties with Baghdad.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Kurd leader to drop ties with Baghdad.

text.p: A senior U.S. diplomat urged Iraqi Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani on Wednesday to drop his alliance with Baghdad and make peace with a rival Kurdish faction, State Department officials said.

Assistant Secretary of State Robert Pelletreau met Barzani, leader of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), for several hours at a secret location in the Turkish capital Ankara, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

The meeting represented a first U.S. attempt to recover lost ground after the KDP invited Iraqi forces to help it rout the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and seize control of most of Western-protected northern Iraq late last month.

The KDP move was seen as restoring to Baghdad a major foothold in the northern Kurdish region from which it has effectively been excluded since Western powers imposed a no-fly zone there after defeating Iraq in the 1991 Gulf War.

"Ambassador Pelletreau raised many of the core issues that have concerned the United States since the outbreak of this crisis, having to do with the situation of the two major Kurdish factions and the feuding between them," Burns said.

"We don't see that the Iraqi Kurds can profit in the long term from an association with (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein. In fact on the contrary we think that such a relationship would be detrimental," he continued. "We hope very much that Mr. Barzani's alliance with Iraq is a one-shot deal."
A diplomat from the British embassy in Ankara and a Turkish government observer also attended what Burns called "a very productive meeting."
Burns declined to give a detailed account of the talks. "This is a very sensitive situation ... We're re-establishing a channel with someone who is a very important leader in northern Iraq," he said.

But he confirmed that the U.S. position spelled out repeatedly over recent days -- stressing the need for the KDP and PUK to negotiate and sever ties with Iraq and Iran respectively -- formed the basis of Pelletreau's agenda.

A KDP spokesman said on Tuesday that Barzani planned to tell Pelletreau that his alliance with Baghdad was only temporary and that he wanted the Western allies to continue an air operation, based in Turkey, to protect the Kurds from Saddam.
A written statement by Burns said Pelletreau held a separate meeting in Ankara with a leader of the Iraqi Turkmen community.

The two meetings covered "continuing U.S. interest in contributing to peace and stability in the region and U.S. concerns about the humanitarian situation of the Kurds, Turkmen, Assyrians and others who live in the region, as well as concerns about the safety of those affiliated with our operations there," it said.
The United States this week airlifted to the United States more than 2,100 people, mainly Kurds, who had worked for U.S. humanitarian programs in northern Iraq.
But others, including members of the U.S.-backed Iraqi National Congress opposition movement, remain stranded in northern Iraq.
Burns said the United States looked forward to further contacts with Barzani in the near future. It was also in touch with PUK leader Jalal Talabani in an attempt to arrange a meeting with him.
Pelletreau is due to return to Washington on Thursday.
